briefs.author_statement: Extract the first-hop interaction sequence of a node and encode it using node, edge, absolute temporal, and co-occurrence signals. Pass the aligned encoding through a continuous SSM that has been redesigned to make forgetting depend on the elapsed timespan and to selectively attend to important past inputs. Redefine the SSM step size Δt as a learnable, monotonically increasing function of the time gap, inspired by Ebbinghaus’ forgetting curve. Initialize the state transition matrix A as a diagonal matrix with negative real-part eigenvalues to guarantee stable exponential decay with increasing timespan. Redefine B and C as input-dependent matrices with spectral norm constraints, allowing the model to review important historical interactions while suppressing noise. For link prediction, use two independent DyG-Mamba encoders for source and destination nodes, pool their outputs, concatenate, and apply an MLP predictor; for node classification, use a single encoder without co-occurrence encoding.

mechanism_draft.text: Mechanism sketch for the mainline algorithm step. The pipeline proceeds in three phases. Phase 1 (Encoding): For a target node, extract the ordered first-hop neighbor interaction sequence up to the prediction timestamp. Each interaction event is represented by a tuple of node identity, edge features, absolute interaction time, and co-occurrence context. The sequence is padded to a fixed maximum length and split into patches of a fixed size. Padded multi-channel data (node, edge, temporal, co-occurrence channels) are stacked along a new dimension to form a unified tensor. A learned router produces per-patch logits that are normalized via softmax to yield routing weights; a top-k selection retains the highest-scoring patches, and a weighted sum over the selected patches produces a compact node embedding. For link prediction, two independent encoder instances process the source and destination sequences separately; their outputs are pooled, concatenated, and passed through an MLP predictor. For node classification, a single encoder is used without the co-occurrence channel. Phase 2 (Timespan-Aware SSM): The aligned encoding is passed through a continuous-state-space model whose step size Δt is redefined as a learnable, monotonically increasing function of the elapsed time gap between consecutive interactions, inspired by the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve. The state transition matrix A is initialized as a diagonal matrix whose eigenvalues have negative real parts, guaranteeing that the state decays exponentially as the timespan grows. The input matrix B and output matrix C are redefined as input-dependent (i.e., functions of the current hidden state) with spectral norm constraints, so the model can selectively reinforce important historical interactions while suppressing noise. The intended mathematical role: Δt(τ) is a scalar function of the inter-event gap τ such that larger gaps produce larger Δt, which in turn causes the discrete-time state update to forget more of the previous state; the diagonal A with negative eigenvalues ensures the continuous-time decay factor exp(A·Δt) contracts toward zero as Δt increases. Phase 3 (Readout): Fixed-size node embeddings are read out from the sequential output and fed into task-specific heads. Supported facets: the padding, stacking, routing, top-k, and weighted-pooling operations are directly evidenced in the repository. Partially supported / author-intent facets: the SSM redesign (Δt redefinition, A initialization, B/C input-dependence with spectral norm) describes the intended mathematical role of the MambaTimeDelta module; the specific spectral norm constraint and Ebbinghaus-inspired monotonicity are design choices not directly visible in the provided fragments.
mechanism_draft.caveat: The SSM redesign facets (timespan-dependent Δt, diagonal A initialization, input-dependent B/C with spectral norm) are author-intent claims not directly evidenced in the provided fragments; they describe the intended mathematical role of the MambaTimeDelta component. The encoding pipeline and task-specific readout are supported by repository fragments.

mechanism_draft.text: Mechanism sketch for the dynamic graph encoding stage. Raw interaction sequences are transformed into a unified, aligned feature representation that captures both temporal and structural context. Concretely: (1) For each target node, the first-hop neighbor events are collected and padded to a fixed sequence length. Multi-channel features (node identity, edge attributes, absolute timestamps, co-occurrence indicators) are assembled into a tensor of shape [batch, sequence_length, num_channels × channel_embedding_dim]. (2) The padded data are stacked along a new dimension to produce a 3-D tensor. (3) A learned router computes per-position logits; these are normalized via softmax to produce routing weights that sum to one over the sequence dimension. (4) A top-k selection retains the k highest-scoring positions (capped at the actual sequence length), and a weighted sum over the selected positions yields a compact embedding. The intended mathematical role of the channel combination: each channel contributes a learned embedding that is combined (via element-wise product or concatenation followed by a linear projection) to form a joint representation; the product form allows the model to learn interactions between channels (e.g., how edge type modulates the effect of temporal proximity). The output is a pair of node embeddings (source and destination) ready for downstream SSM processing. All operations in this stage are supported by the repository fragments.

briefs.author_statement: Timespan-aware forgetting in SSM: Let the SSM forget historical states proportionally to the elapsed time by making Δt a function of the timespan and initializing A for stable decay.

mechanism_draft.text: Mechanism sketch for the timespan-aware forgetting stage within the SSM. The MambaTimeDelta module receives the aligned encoding from the previous stage and processes it through a continuous-state-space recurrence. The forward pass branches on whether time-aware mode is active and whether a time-delta tensor (dts) is provided. When active, the input is projected via a learned weight matrix and reshaped from [batch, length, dim] to [dim, batch × length] for the SSM scan. The key design choice: the step size Δt is not a fixed scalar but a learnable, monotonically increasing function of the inter-event time gap τ. The intended mathematical role: Δt(τ) = f(τ) where f is a monotone-increasing function (e.g., a softplus or exponential of a learned affine transform of τ), so that larger gaps produce larger effective step sizes. The state transition matrix A is initialized as a diagonal matrix with negative real-part eigenvalues, ensuring that the continuous-time decay factor exp(A·Δt) contracts the state toward zero as Δt grows, implementing a forgetting proportional to elapsed time. The input matrix B and output matrix C are made input-dependent (functions of the current hidden state) with spectral norm constraints to bound the gain and prevent instability. The forward pass computes the SSM scan, applies a gating mechanism (element-wise product of the scan output with a gated projection), and returns the processed output. The weighted-sum aggregation of contributing terms is performed over the sequence dimension. Supported facets: the branching logic, projection, and gating operations are evidenced in the repository. Author-intent facets: the specific form of f(τ), the diagonal A initialization, and the spectral norm constraints describe the intended mathematical role and are not directly visible in the provided fragments.

The specific mathematical form of Δt(τ), the diagonal A initialization, and the spectral norm constraints on B/C are author-intent design choices; the provided fragments show the control flow and projection operations but not the closed-form decay equation.

mechanism_draft.text: The motivation section identifies two key limitations of vanilla state-space models when applied to dynamic graphs. First, standard SSMs assume uniform timesteps and therefore ignore the irregular timespans that characterize real-world interaction sequences. Second, the state update in a vanilla SSM has no explicit mechanism to suppress unreliable or noisy transitions, making the model vulnerable to input noise. These limitations motivate the timespan-aware and noise-robust design choices that follow.
